title: Wave properties and types
keyIdea: A wave carries energy from place to place without carrying the material along. It has an amplitude, a wavelength, a frequency and a speed, linked by v = f × λ. Transverse waves wiggle across the direction of travel; longitudinal waves wiggle along it.

kid: Flick one end of a rope and a bump runs along it. The rope stays where it is. Only the wave moves on, carrying energy.
Amplitude is how far a bit of rope moves from the middle. Wavelength is the length of one whole wave, crest to crest. Frequency is how many waves pass each second, in hertz (Hz).
Speed = frequency × wavelength. If 3 waves pass each second and each is 2 m long, the wave moves 6 m each second.
On a rope the bits move up and down, across the way the wave goes. That is a transverse wave. In sound, the air moves back and forth along the way the wave goes. That is a longitudinal wave.
adult: Waves transfer energy, not matter: each particle oscillates about a fixed position. In transverse waves (light, water ripples, waves on a string) the oscillation is perpendicular to the direction of travel; in longitudinal waves (sound, a pushed slinky) it is parallel, giving compressions and rarefactions.

The speed is set by the medium, not by the source. Wiggle faster and the frequency rises, so each wave must be shorter: v = f × λ, with v in m/s, f in Hz and λ in metres. Amplitude is independent of all three.
Common slips: measuring the wavelength from a crest to the next trough (that is half a wavelength), and calling the peak-to-trough height the amplitude (that is twice it).

familyTip: Tie a rope or a skipping rope to a door handle. Take turns wiggling slowly, then fast. Count the waves you can see each time. Faster wiggles give more, shorter waves.

practice.prompt: A duck sits on a pond as ripples pass under it. What does the duck do?
choices: Bobs up and down but stays in about the same place
Is carried along to the edge by the ripples
practice.hint: Do waves carry the water along, or just the energy?
practice.explain: The water, and the duck, just bob up and down. The ripples carry energy across the pond, not the water.

practice.prompt: A wave has a frequency of {f} Hz and a wavelength of {l} m. What is its speed in m/s?
Which of these is a longitudinal wave?
practice.hint: In which one do the particles move back and forth along the direction of travel?
practice.explain: Sound: the air is squashed and stretched along the direction the sound travels. Light and ripples are transverse.

practice.prompt: Waves on a rope travel at {=v*2} m/s. You wiggle the end {v} times a second. How long is each wave, in metres?

pool.prompt: A sound wave has frequency {=f*10} Hz and wavelength {l} m. What is its speed in m/s?
You wiggle a rope twice as often, with the same tension. What happens to the wavelength?
pool.hint: The rope sets the speed, and v = f × λ.
pool.explain: The speed is fixed by the rope. Double f means λ must halve so that f × λ stays the same.

pool.prompt: On a diagram, the distance from a crest to the next trough is 0.5 m. What is the wavelength?
pool.hint: Crest to trough is only part of a full wave.
pool.explain: Crest to trough is half a wave, so the wavelength is 2 × 0.5 = 1 m.

pool.prompt: A wave travels at {=l*f} m/s with a wavelength of {l} m. What is its frequency in Hz?
Which change makes a wave on a rope carry more energy without changing its wavelength?
pool.hint: Which property changes the height but not the length of the waves?
pool.explain: A bigger amplitude: the rope moves further from the middle, which takes more energy. Wavelength depends on frequency and speed only.

pool.prompt: In a transverse wave, the particles move…
choices: at right angles to the direction the wave travels
along the direction the wave travels
along with the wave to the end
pool.hint: Think of the red bead on the rope.
pool.explain: At right angles: the rope moves up and down while the wave moves along.

pool.prompt: What do the 'compressions' in a sound wave mean?
choices: Places where the air particles are squashed close together
The highest points of the wave
Places with no air at all
pool.hint: Look at the slinky: some coils bunch up.
pool.explain: Compressions are where the particles crowd together; rarefactions are where they spread apart.

visual.caption: Change the amplitude, frequency and speed until your wave matches the faint target wave.

lab.caption: Flagship lab: the wave rope. Wiggle it yourself, measure a wavelength, and turn it into a slinky.
